reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission caused by antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels that reduce acetylcholine release
Presents with proximal limb weakness, especially the legs, together with autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation, and erectile dysfunction
Strength may transiently improve with sustained or repeated effort (post-exercise facilitation), and depressed reflexes can augment after exercise
Ocular and bulbar symptoms are usually milder than in myasthenia gravis, though some overlap occurs
About half of cases are paraneoplastic, most often linked to small-cell lung cancer, and may precede the tumour diagnosis
Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a low baseline compound muscle action potential with decrement at low frequency and marked increment at high frequency or after exercise
Treatment addresses any underlying tumour and enhances acetylcholine release; immunotherapy is used for symptom control
A validated screening score helps stratify the likelihood of underlying small-cell lung cancer and guides surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: In LEMS, IgG autoantibodies target P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic motor nerve terminal. Reduced calcium influx during depolarisation diminishes the quantal release of acetylcholine, so the endplate potential often fails to reach threshold at rest, causing weakness. Repeated activity allows calcium to accumulate in the terminal, temporarily augmenting release and improving strength, which explains facilitation. The same antibodies act on autonomic ganglia and terminals, producing cholinergic autonomic failure. In paraneoplastic cases the tumour expresses calcium channels that trigger the cross-reactive immune response.
additionalInvestigations: Serum antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Repetitive nerve stimulation at low and high frequency and post-exercise testing
CT of the chest and, if negative, FDG-PET to search for small-cell lung cancer
Interval tumour surveillance imaging when initial screening is negative but risk is high
SOX1 antibodies as a marker supporting an underlying small-cell lung cancer
Single-fibre electromyography in equivocal neuromuscular transmission cases
redFlags: Any new diagnosis should trigger a directed search for occult malignancy, especially small-cell lung cancer
Weight loss, haemoptysis, or a smoking history increasing suspicion of underlying tumour
Progressive bulbar or respiratory weakness requiring monitoring of airway and ventilation
Severe autonomic failure causing symptomatic hypotension or gastrointestinal stasis
reference.prognosis: Symptoms often improve with treatment of any underlying cancer and with therapies that enhance acetylcholine release; the overall outlook is dominated by the associated malignancy when present, whereas non-paraneoplastic disease tends to follow a more indolent, manageable course.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing LEMS as myasthenia gravis and missing the search for lung cancer
Stopping tumour surveillance too early after an initially negative chest scan
Overlooking autonomic symptoms that are an important diagnostic clue
Failing to appreciate post-exercise facilitation on examination and electrophysiology
Attributing proximal weakness to a primary myopathy without neuromuscular junction testing
management: Start symptomatic treatment with amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) to enhance presynaptic acetylcholine release, adding pyridostigmine where helpful
Search for and treat underlying small-cell lung cancer, since successful tumour treatment often improves the neurological syndrome
Use immunotherapy - corticosteroids, azathioprine, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange or rituximab - for disabling or refractory weakness
Continue interval tumour surveillance with CT and FDG-PET when initial screening is negative but malignancy risk remains high
Provide supportive care including physiotherapy and symptomatic treatment of autonomic features such as dry mouth and constipation
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, oncology and respiratory medicine
Escalate and monitor ventilation if severe, bulbar or respiratory weakness develops
